To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the number of protein families in genomes scales sublinearly with genome size and that the number of domain classes in genomes scales as the number of proteins or domains.
the number of protein domain families is sub-linear in the genome size, and that the number of families of each domain class scales as a power-law of genome size.

(i) a stochastic model of protein universe evolution, based on a few simple parameters, is able to reproduce the statistical distributions of domain classes and domain families in many genomes; (ii) the model is robust to selective pressures, as shown by the ability to fit the data for hundreds of genomes, with a wide range of sizes, with a single set of parameters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the statistical description of protein domains, the units of structure and function of proteins, and their evolution.
the evolution of the universe of protein domains.
the evolution of protein domains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evolution of the protein domain universe is a process of self-organization, in which the role of selection is to regulate the relative abundance of domain classes, while the time-scale of innovation is constrained by a universal minimal number of domains.

the evolution of the protein universe is dominated by the interplay between two processes: (i) a stochastic process of growth and diversification, with two universal parameters (the minimal number of domains per protein and the relative time-scales of innovation and duplication) and (ii) selective pressure acting both as a global constrain on the time-scale of innovation and as a regulator on the population of specific domains classes.
the evolution of the protein universe is a self-organizing process, in which selection plays the role of a regulator, but not of a driver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the protein universe has a modular structure, and that it evolves according to simple rules that are not affected by the complexity of life.

the evolution of the protein universe is a process of growth of a complex network with a very high degree of modularity, which is driven by two main forces: a universal growth mechanism, which is a consequence of the physical nature of protein domains, and selective pressures which are specific to the context.
evolution of proteins is a complex, hierarchical process, where selection is a global, emergent property.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the evolutionary process is dominated by the interplay between two fundamental forces, the thermodynamic origin of protein structures (and their stability) and the need for biological diversity (and the need for modularity in protein structures).

a simple, thermodynamic model of domain evolution can reproduce the main statistical properties of the protein universe and that the resulting model can be used to make quantitative predictions on the evolution of protein functions.
a very limited set of rules can explain a very complex phenomenon.
